accroche: Epictetus was born a slave. His philosophy is not a performance tool: it is what was left to him.
contenu_vulgarise:
Epictetus's *Manual* opens with a distinction, and everything else follows from it: there are things that are up to us, and things that are not.

Up to us are our judgments, our intentions, our desires, our aversions, the use we make of what happens to us. Not up to us are our body, our reputation, our possessions, the position we hold. Epictetus adds that unhappiness consists precisely in being mistaken about this boundary: wanting to master what escapes us, and neglecting what is within reach.

## Who Is Writing This

Epictetus was born a slave, around the year 50, in Phrygia. He belonged to a freedman of Nero. He limps; ancient sources differ on the cause. Freed, then banished from Rome by Domitian, he ended his life at Nicopolis, in Epirus, where he taught. He wrote nothing himself: the *Manual* and the *Discourses* are notes taken by his student Arrian.

This detail is not decorative. The dichotomy of control is not a piece of optimization advice given by someone who had a choice. It is what remains when one has, literally, no power over one's own condition.

## What the Contemporary Version Removes

Stoicism is now widely quoted in performance circles: keep your calm, focus on what you control, do not waste energy on the rest. The reading is faithful. It is also truncated.

What disappears is the framework. For the Stoics, the distinction rests on a physics: the world is governed by a rational order, and accepting what is not up to us means aligning oneself with that order, not gaining efficiency. Remove the metaphysics and what is left is a stress-management technique, stripped of what gave it its meaning.

An uncomfortable political consequence follows. If the injustice one suffers is not up to us, must one merely endure it? Epictetus leans toward acceptance. That is consistent with the rest of his doctrine, and it is exactly what he has been reproached for ever since.

## What This Shifts

The dichotomy does not diminish what happens to you and promises no relief. It shifts the question: no longer “how do I get what I want,” but “what can I want that does not depend on luck.” The answer is narrow, and accepting it costs more than the quotations in circulation let on.

carte.punch: Stoicism has become a productivity method. Epictetus was a slave.
carte.idee: His distinction between what is up to us and what is not is not optimization advice: it is what remains when one has no power over one's own condition. The modern version removes the metaphysics, and the politics.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: On what modern reception leaves aside.

quiz.question: What does the contemporary reading of Stoicism most often leave aside?
choix: The metaphysical framework: to accept is to align oneself with a rational order of the world
The idea that our judgments and desires are indeed up to us
The fact that the doctrine was aimed first at rulers and men of power
The very distinction between what is up to us and what is not
quiz.explication: The modern version keeps the technique, focusing on what one controls, but abandons what grounded it: a physics in which the world follows a rational order that one aligns oneself with. Without that framework, the dichotomy becomes a stress-management tool. Epictetus, a former slave, was moreover not addressing the powerful.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the text, what is up to us in Epictetus's distinction?
choix: Our judgments, our intentions, and the use we make of what happens to us
Our reputation and the position we hold
External events and their direct consequences
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Epictetus places on the side of what is up to us our judgments, our intentions, our desires, our aversions, and the use we make of what happens to us. The body, reputation, and possessions are not up to us.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who wrote the Manual and the Discourses attributed to Epictetus?
choix: Epictetus himself, late in life, at Nicopolis
A freedman of Nero's court, to whom Epictetus belonged
Domitian, who supposedly had it recorded before banishing him from Rome
His student Arrian, from notes taken during Epictetus's teaching
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Epictetus wrote nothing himself: the Manual and the Discourses are notes taken by his student Arrian, who gave form to his master's oral teaching.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What position does Epictetus take toward an injustice suffered, according to the entry?
choix: He calls for fighting it by every means, since justice is up to us
He leans toward acceptance, since the injustice one suffers is not up to us
He distinguishes legal injustices, to be fought, from moral injustices, to be accepted
He refuses to take a position, the question being outside the scope of his philosophy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: If the injustice one suffers is not up to us, Epictetus leans toward acceptance, a consequence consistent with the rest of his doctrine but one that has earned him a steady political reproach ever since.
